questions.question: 1. Which of the following arrays represents a valid min-heap after the insert-heap step is performed?

explanations.a: Correct. Every parent is less than or equal to its children in this array, so it satisfies the min-heap property.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The node with value 3 has a child with a smaller value, so the min-heap property is violated.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The root value is larger than one of its children, so the min-heap property is violated.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The node with value 1 is valid as the root, but the node with value 9 has a child smaller than itself, violating the min-heap property.

questions.question: 2. What do you think is the complexity of inserting into a heap using this naive insert heap method? (Consider if it can be further improved)

explanations.a: Correct. In the naive method described in the experiment, an insertion may require shifting or scanning a linear number of elements, giving $O(n)$ time. A heap insertion can be improved to $O(\log n)$ with the standard sift-up approach.
explanations.b: Incorrect. $O(\log n)$ describes the standard efficient heap insertion based on moving the new element along the heap height, not the naive method described here.
explanations.c: Incorrect. $O(n\log n)$ is not the cost of a single insertion in this context.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The naive insertion described does not require a quadratic amount of work for one insertion.

questions.question: 3. In a min-heap, where should a newly inserted element initially be placed before restoring the heap property?

answers.c: At the next available position at the end of the heap
answers.d: Always as the left child of the root

explanations.a: Incorrect. Directly placing a new element at the root could disrupt the complete-tree structure.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A heap must maintain its complete binary tree shape, so arbitrary placement is not allowed.
explanations.c: Correct. The new element is first placed at the next available position at the end of the heap, then moved upward as needed.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The insertion position depends on the current complete-tree shape and is not always the left child of the root.

questions.question: 4. What operation is used to restore the heap property after inserting a new element?

explanations.a: Correct. After insertion, the new element may violate the heap property with its parent, so it is repeatedly moved upward until the property is restored.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Merge is associated with combining sorted sequences, not repairing a heap after insertion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Partition is a step used in Quick Sort, not standard heap insertion.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Linear search finds a value but does not restore the heap property.

questions.question: 5. If the height of a binary heap is $O(\log n)$, what is the worst-case time complexity of standard heap insertion using sift-up?

explanations.a: Incorrect. In the worst case, the inserted element may move through several levels.
explanations.b: Correct. Sift-up can move the new element along at most the heap height, which is $O(\log n)$.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sift-up follows one path through the heap rather than scanning all $n$ elements.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The number of levels traversed during one insertion is logarithmic, not quadratic.

questions.question: 6. Why is the complete-tree property important during heap insertion?

answers.a: It ensures every element has the same value
answers.b: It guarantees the array is sorted
answers.c: It determines a valid next position while keeping the heap shape complete
answers.d: It removes the need for comparisons

explanations.a: Incorrect. Completeness concerns the tree's shape, not equality of values.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A heap is not required to be globally sorted like an array.
explanations.c: Correct. The complete-tree property determines where the new node is placed so the heap retains its required shape.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Comparisons are still needed to restore the heap-order property after insertion.

questions.question: 7. Suppose a min-heap contains the elements $[2, 4, 6, 8]$. If $1$ is inserted and sift-up is performed, what will be the new root?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The inserted value is smaller than the current root, so the root cannot remain unchanged after all required upward adjustments.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This value is not the smallest among the elements after insertion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This value is larger than several elements and cannot become the root of a min-heap.
explanations.d: Correct. Since $1$ is smaller than every existing element, sift-up moves it to the root.

questions.question: 8. Which statement best distinguishes the naive insert-heap method from the standard efficient heap insertion?

answers.a: The naive method never changes the array
answers.b: The standard method maintains the complete-tree shape and restores order along a root-to-leaf path in $O(\log n)$ worst-case time
answers.c: The naive method always takes $O(n^2)$ for one insertion
answers.d: The standard method requires sorting the entire array after every insertion

explanations.a: Incorrect. Both approaches can rearrange elements as part of insertion.
explanations.b: Correct. Standard heap insertion places the new element at the next available position and restores the heap property by moving it upward along at most the heap height.
explanations.c: Incorrect. One insertion in the naive method does not inherently require quadratic work.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Efficient heap insertion does not require sorting the entire array after each insertion.

questions.question: 9. If $n$ elements are inserted one at a time into a heap using the standard $O(\log n)$ insertion method, what is the worst-case upper bound for all insertions?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This is smaller than the total obtained when logarithmic-time insertion is performed repeatedly.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This is the bound for a single insertion, not a sequence of $n$ insertions.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The standard insertion method does not require $O(n)$ work for each insertion.
explanations.d: Correct. $n$ insertions with up to $O(\log n)$ work each give an overall worst-case bound of $O(n\log n)$.
